chunks: Slope compensation and when it's needed. The question: What is slope compensation and when is it needed? (what kinda person asks undergrads this?)
Slope compensation is a small artificial ramp added to the current signal in a peak current mode converter.
It makes the switch turn off a little earlier when the current started too high. Without it, the converter oscillates in an unstable pattern whenever the duty cycle is above 50%.
With enough ramp, it is stable at any duty cycle.
Imagine filling a bathtub and shutting the tap when the water reaches a marked line. Now suppose that line slowly sinks while you fill.
If the tub started fuller than usual, the water meets the sinking line sooner, so you add less water this cycle. That extra correction calms the error down.
If the line sinks too steeply, though, the line decides when you stop more than the water does, and you lose the benefit of watching the current.
The multiplier against duty. Without a ramp it falls below -1 at D equals 0. 5 . With m a equals 0.
5m 2 it stays within plus or minus 1 for all duty cycles (reaching -1 only as D to 1 ) and with m a equals m 2 it is zero everywhere.
Rising slope m 1 : how fast the inductor current climbs while the switch is on. Falling slope m 2 : how fast it drops while the switch is off.
Compensation ramp m a : the artificial slope that we add.
Subharmonic oscillation: alternating long and short pulses at half the switching frequency ("Peak current mode below and above 50% duty").
Duty cycle (D): the fraction of the period the switch is on.
Peak current mode: control that turns the switch off when the measured inductor current reaches a target ("Voltage mode vs current mode control").
Take V in equals 4 volts, V out equals 3 volts and L equals 1 microhenries. Then D equals 0. 75 , m 1 equals 1 amps/µs and m 2 equals 3 amps/µs.
With no ramp, each error is multiplied by -m 2 over m 1 equals -3 , so it grows. Add a ramp of m a equals 1. 5 amps/µs (half of m 2 ). The multiplier becomes -(3-1.
5) over (1 plus 1. 5) equals -0. 6 , so errors shrink. With m a equals 3 amps/µs it becomes 0, and an error is gone in one cycle. That is the whole idea.
"Slope compensation is an artificial ramp added to the sensed inductor current in fixed-frequency peak current-mode control.
Without it, an error in the inductor current is multiplied by D over one minus D every cycle, so above 50 percent duty it grows into subharmonic oscillation.
With a ramp of slope m a the multiplier becomes minus m2 minus m a over m1 plus m a, so a ramp of at least half the inductor's down-slope makes it stable at any duty cycle.
Too much ramp pushes the converter toward voltage mode and lowers the peak current limit at high duty cycle."
